lesson.title: The Poet Who Wrote Harlem: Langston Hughes
lesson.summary: Langston Hughes became the most celebrated poet of the Harlem Renaissance by writing about ordinary Black life in the rhythms of jazz and blues, insisting that Black artists had no obligation to please white or Black audiences alike.
lesson.body:
Langston Hughes was born in 1901 in Joplin, Missouri, and spent much of his childhood being raised by his grandmother in Lawrence, Kansas, after his parents separated. As a teenager he began writing poetry, and in 1921, while riding a train across the Mississippi River to visit his father in Mexico, he wrote what became his first major published poem, The Negro Speaks of Rivers, which appeared that year in The Crisis, the NAACP magazine edited by W.E.B. Du Bois. Hughes briefly attended Columbia University but left after a year, frustrated by the racism he encountered there, and instead threw himself into the literary and cultural life of nearby Harlem. He later completed his degree at Lincoln University in Pennsylvania in 1929.

Hughes's public breakthrough came through an almost accidental encounter. Working as a busboy at a Washington, D.C. hotel in 1925, he left several of his poems beside the plate of the well known poet Vachel Lindsay, who was dining there. Lindsay was impressed enough to read Hughes's poems aloud at his own public reading that same night and publicized the discovery of a talented young Black poet, bringing Hughes national attention almost overnight. The following year Hughes published his first full length poetry collection, The Weary Blues, in 1926, a title that pointed toward the defining feature of his style.

What set Hughes apart from many of his literary contemporaries was his commitment to writing in the actual rhythms and voice of everyday Black working class life, borrowing the cadences of blues and jazz music directly into his verse rather than imitating traditional European poetic forms. He made this artistic philosophy explicit in his influential 1926 essay The Negro Artist and the Racial Mountain, arguing that Black artists should feel free to express themselves honestly without worrying whether white audiences approved or whether more conservative members of the Black middle class found their subject matter too common. This insistence on authenticity, on writing about the lives of porters, dancers, and laborers rather than only the polished and respectable, made Hughes both controversial and beloved in his own time, and it cemented his lasting reputation as the poet who gave the Harlem Renaissance its most distinctive voice.
